title: Water use, drainage and environmental control
audience: Cleaners and contractors working on food-processing sites where wash water and high-pressure devices are used.
learningOutcomes: Trace where wash water could reach drains, production areas and the environment.
Recognise aerosol, drainage overflow and slip hazards from wet cleaning and high-pressure devices.
Stop and escalate for unapproved water use, and record the hold.

instruction.heading: Where the water goes
instruction.body: Wash water on a food-processing site can reach floor drains, product areas, equipment and surfaces that contact food, wastewater systems, and, where a drain connects outside, stormwater. Trace each path before you use water. Start from the point where the water is applied and follow it to the floor, then to the nearest drain, then to the point where the drain goes. Check whether the drain has the capacity for the volume you will use, and check the drain map the site holds. A drain that backs up or overflows can carry contamination back into a production area, and water that runs toward ingredients, packaging or equipment is a contamination pathway in its own right. If you cannot trace the path, treat it as unknown and do not use water there until the site has confirmed it. Food safety law in Australia requires food premises and equipment to be kept clean and sanitary, and the FSANZ guidance on cleaning and sanitising under Standard 3.2.2 describes the sequence of rinsing, washing and sanitising. Water is part of that sequence, so its path matters as much as the cleaning method.

instruction.heading: Aerosols and high-pressure devices
instruction.body: High-pressure and spray devices create aerosols, which are fine droplets that can carry soil and micro-organisms into the air and onto surfaces that are not being cleaned. This is the main reason spray is restricted near open product. Use water-based methods only where the site instruction permits them, and keep spray away from exposed product, open containers, packaging and open equipment. Consider the aerosol path as well as the floor path: a jet that is safe at the floor can still carry droplets onto a nearby surface. Floors become slippery when wet. The SafeWork NSW guidance notes that cleaning products and methods can leave floors slippery, and that poor drainage lets liquid pool, so the controls are containment of spills, floor maintenance and drainage, and non-slip footwear in wet conditions. The use of barriers and drying as additional controls is site practice, not a requirement stated in that guidance.

instruction.heading: Environmental controls and discharge
instruction.body: Wash water, detergent residues and rinse water can reach waste systems and the environment. In Victoria, EPA guidance says that waste should be kept out of stormwater drains so far as reasonably practicable, and that the general duty applies to wastewater as well as to other waste (EPA Victoria, updated 7 May 2025). Discharging trade waste into a sewer also has its own approval rules. A Victorian water corporation states that businesses must have a trade waste consent or agreement before discharging trade waste to the sewer, and that discharging without one is an offence (Goulburn Valley Water, a Victorian water corporation). Before using a detergent or a cleaning product in a drain or near one, check the site's approval and the product's SDS, and do not assume that a product is acceptable to discharge.

instruction.heading: Food safety program status
instruction.body: A food safety program under Standard 3.2.1 applies to food businesses that the enforcing agency has placed in a priority classification, and the classification is decided under state or territory law. The FSANZ guide to Standard 3.2.1, a first edition from June 2007, explains this. The guide is explanatory and is not the standard, so the clauses of the standard itself govern. Because the guide is dated 2007, its statements about which jurisdictions require a program are historical. This lesson does not confer any food safety clearance or qualification, and it does not establish that a site is compliant.

instruction.heading: Stopping, holding and recording
instruction.body: Stop the task where there is aerosol risk, drainage overflow, or water use the site has not approved. Do not look for a workaround, and do not use more pressure to clear a drain. Escalate to the responsible authorised person, protect the area and any exposed product, and record the hold, the referral and the pending decision. Protecting exposed product means covering it or keeping people away from it, and any move of product is for the authorised person to decide. Do not record the area as clean, safe, sanitised or released. Those statements are decisions for the authorised person, based on checks you did not make.

procedure: Trace the path of wash water to drains, product areas, equipment and any environmental interface before use.
Check drain capacity, the drain map and the site's water-use instruction before any water is applied.
Keep spray and high-pressure devices away from exposed product, open containers and open equipment, and use only the method the site permits.
Contain spills and keep the floor drained and maintained, and require non-slip footwear in wet areas.
Stop and escalate on aerosol risk, overflow or unapproved water use, protect the area, and record the hold and referral without any clearance claim.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is asked to use a high-pressure device on a floor beside open product containers, and the drain is already backing up.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do first, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. High-pressure spray near open product creates an aerosol and contamination risk, and a backing-up drain is a sign of overflow. Do not use more pressure to clear it. Escalate to the authorised person, protect the exposed product in the way the authorised person directs, and keep people away from the area. Record the hold, the referral, the time and the pending decision, without claiming any clearance.

workedExamples.situation: A wet-cleaning method is permitted by the site instruction for a dry-goods store with no exposed product. The floor drain is clear, but the route of the wash water passes close to a packaging line that is still running.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the work start, and under what conditions?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not start until the route is traced and the authorised person has confirmed that the packaging line can be protected from the water and any spray. Use only the method the site instruction specifies, keep barriers and wet-floor signs in place, and check the drain during the work. If water starts to pool, or if any spray reaches the packaging line, stop and escalate as in the previous example.

workedExamples.situation: Wash water is running toward a pallet of packaging materials, and the site drain map is not available at the work point.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the water and do not continue until the route is known. Move the cleaning away from the pallet only if the authorised person agrees, and do not redirect water toward another area on your own judgement. Obtain the drain map through the supervisor, record the hold and the reason, and do not record the packaging as safe or released.

equipmentAndPpe: Site-approved water-use instruction and drain map.
Gloves and eye protection as set by the product SDS and the task risk assessment.
Non-slip footwear suitable for wet areas.
Barriers, wet-floor signs and drying equipment, as the site provides.
Approved detergents and sanitisers, used as the SDS and the site instruction direct.

commonErrors.error: Using high-pressure spray near open product.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not spray near exposed product, and follow the site instruction.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring a slow or backing-up drain.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop and report the overflow before using more water.

commonErrors.error: Recording the area as clean or released after water was used.
commonErrors.prevention: Record only what was done, and leave clearance to the authorised person.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a drain goes to a sewer or to stormwater without checking the drain map.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the drain map and the site instruction before any water use.

commonErrors.error: Using water on a wet floor without signs or containment.
commonErrors.prevention: Place signs and barriers, contain the spill and require non-slip footwear.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Food safety programs under Standard 3.2.1: the FSANZ guide (first edition June 2007) explains that a program applies only to food businesses placed in a priority classification by the enforcing agency under state or territory law. The guide is explanatory and not legally binding. This lesson does not confer any food safety clearance or qualification.

Cleaning and sanitising under Standard 3.2.2: the FSANZ page (last updated 30 September 2025) says that food premises and equipment must be kept clean and sanitary, that food waste, dirt and grease must not be allowed to build up, and that items should be cleaned before they are sanitised. The standard text itself was not read for this lesson.

Discharge and environmental controls: wastewater, trade waste and stormwater are subject to state and territory environmental rules and to water authority arrangements. In Victoria, trade waste discharge to sewer needs a consent or agreement (Goulburn Valley Water), and waste should be kept out of stormwater drains so far as reasonably practicable (EPA Victoria). This lesson does not grant any environmental or discharge permit, consent or agreement.
Slip hazards: the SafeWork NSW guidance (NSW only) treats cleaning products, cleaning methods and poor drainage as causes of slippery floors.

qualityStandard: Water path traced and drain capacity checked against the drain map in the simulated site drawing.
Aerosol, overflow and unapproved-water stop triggers identified in the case study.
Hold and referral recorded in the simulated task, with no clearance or release claim.
Protection of exposed product described as directed by the authorised person, not decided by the cleaner.
documentationEvidence: Water-path and drain check record, with the drain map reference and the site instruction reference.
Hold and referral record with the time, the area, the person notified and the pending decision.
Product exposure note, where any product was near the water or spray.
summary: Trace where the water goes before using it, and check the drain map.
Aerosols, overflow and unapproved water use are stop triggers.
Escalate, protect the area, and record the hold without any clearance claim.
Discharge to sewer or stormwater may need approval; do not assume it is allowed.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must water paths be traced before use on a food site?
options: To save water, since the cleaning uses less of it overall on the site
Because water can carry contamination to product, drains and the environment
Because water on a food site is always clean and needs no checks at all

knowledgeChecks.question: A drain is backing up while you plan to use high-pressure water. What is the right action?
options: Use more pressure to clear it before the shift starts
Stop, protect the area and escalate the overflow
Ignore it, because it will drain later on its own

knowledgeChecks.question: What must the record never say?
options: That the work was stopped and why, along with the time of the stop
The name of the person notified about the hold and the time they were told
That the area is sanitised or released when no authorised person has said so
